teaser: A breakfast table in wartime Paris, with a bull hiding among the cups and bottles.
review_notes:
Hidden bull's head (cup as snout, concentric circle as eye, Bass bottle as ear, guitar outline as horn) follows the Metropolitan Museum's published reading: verify wording.
Sale at Christie's London, February 2014, for about 34.8 million pounds (around 57 million dollars), then a record for Gris; the Met announced it as the buyer later that year (Leonard A. Lauder funds): verify.
Picasso's Bull's Head (bicycle seat and handlebars) dated 1942.
The letters 'eau' are read as the end of a wine label such as 'Bordeaux': an interpretation.
Bass's red diamond trademark used here on an 'Extra Stout' label, as legible in the image.
Size 116.5 x 89.2 cm.

lesson.text: In 1942 Pablo Picasso fixed a bicycle saddle to a pair of handlebars and showed the result as a bull's head. People still smile when they get it. Twenty-seven years earlier, his Montmartre neighbor Juan Gris had already played the same trick, in paint, on a table laid for a late breakfast. Almost nobody noticed for decades.

Start with the table itself, because it is crowded. Gris piles a café's worth of things onto a cloth of green and white checks, and he slices them, tilts them and lets them show through each other. Some are easy to name. Go and collect four of them.

lesson.title: What's on the table
lesson.text: Four objects you can name without any help.

spots.title: The grapes
spots.text: Pale green, round, shaded one by one. They sit in a white footed fruit dish whose stem drops straight down below them. This is the most traditional bit of painting in the whole picture.

spots.title: The wine bottle
spots.text: A dark red glow inside a green rectangle, and under it a scrap of label with the letters “eau”. Probably the tail of a word like Bordeaux. Gris gives you the end and lets you supply the rest.

spots.title: The beer
spots.text: A round label with a red diamond: Bass Extra Stout, an English beer sold in Paris cafés. The bottle around it is split into a green half and a dotted purple half.

spots.title: The newspaper
spots.text: LE JOURNAL, a Paris daily, folded and lying at an angle. The masthead is painted by hand, letter by letter. In 1915 its front page was all war news, which Gris leaves as gray scribble.

lesson.text: Grapes, wine, beer, a paper. Add a coffee cup at the bottom, stemmed glasses, and the curving white outline of a guitar on the left, and you have the full inventory. Every item is a cliché of Cubist still life, the kind of picture Picasso and Georges Braque had been making since about 1908 by breaking objects into flat planes seen from several sides at once.

Bass was one of the first brands to turn up in modern painting. Its labels appear on the bar in Édouard Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère in 1882, and Picasso painted the bottle many times. Gris joins a small tradition of artists advertising the same English brewery for free.

So where is the bull? Gris was Spanish, born in Madrid, and for a Spaniard far from home the animal was close to a signature. He builds it out of the objects you have just met, right in the middle of the table. The easiest way in is the eye: a target of black and white rings.
A bull is staring at you from the table. Tap its eye.

spots.title: The bull's eye
spots.text: Seen from above, it is just the top of a cup or glass. Seen as a face, it is an eye. In English a target's center is literally a bull's-eye, a pun Gris may or may not have known.

lesson.text: Once the eye clicks, the rest follows. The coffee cup at the bottom becomes the muzzle. The dark beer bottle on the right stands up like an ear. The white loops of the guitar on the left swing out like a horn. The head fills the canvas, facing you, and then, the moment you look at the grapes again, it is gone.
Cubism taught painters that one shape can be two things. Gris pushes it further: a whole table can also be a face, depending on what you decide to see.

The year matters. In 1915 Paris was a city at war. French painters like Braque were at the front. Gris, a foreign citizen of a neutral country, stayed, short of money and watched with suspicion. A table of café pleasures was a memory of peacetime as much as a subject.

Gris's dealer, Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler, was German. When war broke out he became an enemy alien in France and went into exile in Switzerland, and his stock of paintings was seized. Gris lost his only steady buyer overnight.

There is a second game going on, about materials. A year or two earlier Gris had been gluing real wallpaper and newsprint onto his canvases. Here nothing is glued. He imitates his own collages in oil paint: fake wood, fake printed cloth, fake speckled paper. Roam around and test the surfaces.

spots.title: Fake wood
spots.text: The table's corner, with grain painted in brown streaks. House decorators used this trick to make cheap pine pass for oak. Braque, trained as a decorator, brought it into Cubism.

spots.title: A field of dots
spots.text: Blue and green specks, borrowed from the dotted technique of painters like Georges Seurat thirty years before. Here they are pure decoration, like a printed wallpaper.

spots.title: The guitar
spots.text: Only a white outline, as if drawn in chalk over everything else. You see through it to the tablecloth and the blue wood behind.

spots.title: The coffee cup
spots.text: A dark opening, a pale cylinder, and a ghostly white outline that has slipped sideways off the cup, like a print out of register. It is also the bull's nose.

spots.title: The cloth changes color
spots.text: Up top the checks are green and white. Here the same cloth turns pink and yellow, as if a different light fell on it. Gris treats the pattern as a sheet he can recolor at will.

spots.title: The pedestal
spots.text: The foot of the fruit dish, half sandy dots and half cool gray. Light side, shadow side: Gris shows both by simply cutting the object down the middle.

lesson.text: Notice how little the color wanders, for all this busyness. Green, a dusty pink, black, white, a few blues. Gris planned his pictures like an architect, on paper, with ruler and compass, before touching the canvas. The checks are his grid. They hold forty fragments in place the way graph paper holds a drawing.

In February 2014 this painting sold at auction in London for about 57 million dollars, at that time the highest price ever paid for a Gris. Later that year the Metropolitan Museum of Art revealed itself as the new owner.

Gris died in 1927, at only 40, and never saw Picasso's bicycle bull. You can decide which is the better joke: the one that takes a second to get, or the one that sat in plain sight on a tablecloth for the better part of a century.

quiz.question: What hidden image has been found in this still life?
quiz.explanation: The cup, bottle, guitar and a ringed circle combine into a bull's face.

quiz.question: Which object serves as the bull's eye?
options: A circle of black and white rings
quiz.explanation: The target-like top of a cup or glass doubles as the eye.

quiz.question: How are the wood grain and printed patterns made in this picture?
quiz.explanation: Nothing is glued here: Gris copies his own collage effects in paint.

quiz.question: Why did Gris lose his dealer in 1914?
options: The dealer was German and had to leave France
The dealer died at the front
quiz.explanation: Kahnweiler became an enemy alien and went into exile in Switzerland.

quiz.question: Which beer brand appears on the table?
quiz.explanation: The round label with a red diamond reads Bass Extra Stout.

facts.text: The newspaper in this painting is a real page pasted onto the canvas.
facts.explanation: The masthead LE JOURNAL is painted by hand; the picture contains no collage.

facts.text: Juan Gris was born in Madrid.
facts.explanation: He was a Spaniard living in Paris, which is one reason the bull mattered to him.

facts.text: Gris painted this table before Picasso made his bicycle-seat Bull's Head.
facts.explanation: The painting dates from 1915; Picasso's sculpture from 1942.
